games.title: Tennis for Two
games.note: Shown at a Brookhaven National Laboratory open house in 1958 on an oscilloscope, with custom aluminum controllers.

games.title: Spacewar!
games.note: Written for MIT's PDP-1. Two ships duel around a star whose gravity pulls them in.

games.title: Galaxy Game
games.note: A coin-operated Spacewar! at Stanford's student union. Only two prototypes were built.

games.title: Computer Space
games.note: The first commercially sold arcade video game. Its curvy fiberglass cabinet appears in the film Soylent Green.

games.title: Space Wars
games.note: Its custom vector hardware became the base for most of Cinematronics' later vector games.

games.title: Star Control
games.dev: Toys for Bob (Paul Reiche III & Fred Ford)
games.note: Paul Reiche III and Fred Ford's first major game together. Its sequel added a large story-driven galaxy.

games.title: Wing Commander
games.note: Cutscenes between missions, and a campaign that branches depending on whether you win or lose.

games.title: Table Tennis (Magnavox Odyssey)
games.note: A ball-and-paddle game on the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console.

games.title: Pong
games.note: The test machine at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale stopped working because its coin box overflowed.

games.title: Breakout
games.dev: Atari (Nolan Bushnell, Steve Bristow, Steve Wozniak)
games.note: Steve Wozniak built the prototype with Steve Jobs, and said designing it shaped features of the Apple II.

games.title: Arkanoid
games.note: Taito's update of Breakout, where your paddle is a spaceship called the Vaus.

games.title: Gee Bee
games.note: Iwatani wanted to make pinball machines. When Namco said no, he made a pinball-style video game.

games.title: Western Gun
games.note: A two-player cowboy duel. Midway rebuilt it with a microprocessor for America as Gun Fight.

games.title: Gun Fight
games.note: Often called the first video game to use a microprocessor, an Intel 8080.

games.title: Space Invaders
games.note: Nishikado built it on Midway's microprocessor board, adding his own boards and circuitry.

games.title: Head On
games.note: Cars circle maze lanes eating dots while dodging a computer car. Japanese writers call it the first dot-eating game.

games.title: Galaxian
games.note: Used full color graphics, and its aliens break formation to dive at the player.

games.title: Galaga
games.note: Enemies can capture your ship with a tractor beam. Rescue it to fly two ships at once.

games.title: Gyruss
games.note: Its music is an arrangement of Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor.
Designer Yoshiki Okamoto later produced Street Fighter II.

games.title: Radar Scope
games.note: It flopped in America, leaving about 2,000 unsold cabinets that Nintendo turned into Donkey Kong.

games.title: Tank
games.note: Sold under Kee Games, a company Atari quietly set up to reach more distributors.

games.title: Combat
games.note: Bundled with most Atari 2600 consoles from 1977 to 1982.

games.title: Battlezone
games.note: The US Army later had Atari build a training version, The Bradley Trainer.

games.title: Star Wars (1983)
games.note: Color vector graphics and digitized voices from the film, building to the Death Star trench run.

links.took: Space combat. Mike Mayfield wanted a Spacewar!-like game that ran on a teleprinter.
links.added: Turn-based text play: hunting Klingons across a galaxy of sectors.

links.took: Rocket-ship space combat. Bushnell had played Spacewar! at the University of Utah.
links.added: A coin-operated cabinet with its own circuits instead of a costly computer.

links.took: The full Spacewar! game, run on a PDP-11 minicomputer.
links.added: A coin slot, so Stanford students paid to play at the student union.

links.took: Two-player ship duels around a star, in vector graphics.
links.added: A commercial arcade cabinet built on Larry Rosenthal's own vector hardware.

links.took: The ship's shape, hyperspace button, control scheme and drifting physics.
links.added: Rocks that split into smaller pieces, and enemy flying saucers.
links.extra: Designer Ed Logg modeled the ship, its five-button controls and its physics on Spacewar!.

links.took: Ship duels around a planet whose gravity pulls them in.
links.added: Fourteen alien ship designs, each with its own weapons, plus a strategy map.

links.took: Bushnell and Dabney's coin-op experience. They founded Atari after Computer Space.
links.added: A simple two-player ping-pong game that anyone could pick up.

links.took: Space-shooting gameplay elements, per the game's history.
links.added: Rocks that break apart, screen-wrapping and a high score table with initials.

links.took: Ball-and-paddle tennis on a TV screen. Bushnell played it in May 1972.
links.added: An on-screen score, sound effects and a coin slot.

src.t: Vintage Computing and Gaming, The Making of Pong

links.extra: Allan Alcorn has said Pong was a direct response to that demo. Magnavox later sued, and Atari paid $700,000 for a license.

links.took: A ball bouncing over a net on an electronic screen.
links.added: A home console that plugged into an ordinary TV.
links.extra: Lawyers tried to use Tennis for Two as prior art against Baer's patents and failed. No source shows Baer drew on it.

links.took: Ball-and-paddle play. Bushnell wanted to turn Pong into a single-player game.
links.added: A wall of bricks to break, so you play against the screen.

src.t: Wikipedia: Breakout, citing Kent, The Ultimate History of Video Games

links.took: Clearing rows of targets from the bottom of the screen. Nishikado wanted to top Breakout.
links.added: Targets that march down and shoot back, with a space invasion theme.

links.took: Breakout's brick-breaking mechanics.
links.added: Pinball bumpers and targets, from Toru Iwatani's love of pinball.

links.took: Bouncing a ball off a paddle to break a wall of bricks.
links.added: Power-up capsules, enemies and many designed stages.

links.took: Toru Iwatani's design. The cute characters of its sequel Cutie Q led to Pac-Man's ghosts.
links.added: A maze full of dots and four ghosts with their own personalities.

links.took: Nishikado's two-player cowboy duel, licensed to Midway.
links.added: An Intel 8080 microprocessor for smoother animation and sharper graphics.

links.took: Microprocessor-run arcade hardware, whose smoother graphics impressed Nishikado.
links.added: Marching aliens on Midway's board plus Nishikado's own added circuits.

links.took: The fixed shooter format. Namco's president demanded a 'post-Invaders' game.
links.added: Full color and aliens that break formation to dive at you.

links.took: Space Invaders' addictive wave-shooting pace, per the game's history.
links.added: Free movement around the whole screen and rocks that split apart.

links.took: The urge to make arcade games. Early prototypes drew heavily on Space Invaders.
links.added: A scrolling planet, a radar map and humanoids to rescue from abductors.

src.t: Wikipedia: Defender, citing a Wired interview with Eugene Jarvis

links.took: Shooting waves of enemies. Theurer 'took Space Invaders and wrapped the surface into a circle'.
links.added: 3D tubes seen from above, color vector graphics and a spinner knob.

links.took: Shooting upward at descending enemies from the bottom of the screen.
links.added: A mushroom field, a trackball and a centipede that splits when hit.

links.took: The shoot 'em up template that Space Invaders set.
links.added: Horizontal scrolling and a power-up bar for choosing upgrades.

links.took: Endless waves of enemies to shoot down.
links.added: Two joysticks, one to move and one to fire in any direction.

links.took: Waves of attacking aliens, which Radar Scope borrowed heavily.
links.added: A tilted 3D-style view looking into the screen.

links.took: Playing round after round instead of against a timer, an idea Sega took from Space Invaders.
links.added: Cars racing around maze lanes, eating dots and dodging a head-on crash.

src.t: Wikipedia: Space Invaders, citing designer Lane Hauck

links.took: The alien-wave shooter formula, built on through Galaxian.
links.added: Tractor beams that steal your ship, and bonus stages.

links.took: Namco's formation shooter with diving alien attacks.
links.added: Captured ships you can win back to fly two fighters side by side.

links.took: Diving Galaxian-style aliens, on hardware first modeled on Namco's Galaxian board.
links.added: A third-person 3D-style perspective that made it look new.

links.took: Designer Kazunori Sawano, who led Galaxian and co-created Pole Position.
links.added: Behind-the-car racing on a real circuit, with a qualifying lap.

links.took: Its unsold cabinets. About 2,000 were converted to run Donkey Kong.
links.added: Miyamoto's first game: a carpenter jumping barrels to rescue a woman from a gorilla.

links.took: Dot collecting in a maze, plus score-boosting items, per historians.
links.added: Four ghosts with personalities, power pellets and cute characters.
links.extra: Namco has not confirmed it. Gremlin co-founder Frank Fogleman believes Pac-Man drew on Head On.

links.took: Galaga-style enemy formations. A critic called it 'Galaga-in-the-round'.
links.added: Flying around a circle toward the screen's center, past the planets.

links.took: Designer Yoshiki Okamoto, who moved from Konami to Capcom.
links.added: A vertical World War II shooter with a loop roll to dodge fire.

links.took: Tank-versus-tank combat. Ed Rotberg called Tank the primary inspiration.
links.added: A first-person 3D view in green wireframe vector graphics.

links.took: Tank duels through mazes, adapted from Atari's own arcade Tank.
links.added: Biplane and jet modes, built in as the Atari 2600's pack-in game.

links.took: First-person 3D shooting, which Battlezone first made a big success.
links.added: Fast texture-mapped corridors, Nazi guards and shareware distribution on PC.

src.t: Wikipedia: Battlezone, citing Hanson, 2021, and Engadget, 2016

links.extra: A genre link only. id Software named other games as its direct inspirations.

links.took: Battlezone's gunner yoke controller and Atari's 3D vector work.
links.added: A first-person Death Star trench run with voices from the film.

src.t: Wikipedia: Battlezone, citing Kent, The Ultimate History of Video Games

links.took: Space game conventions that Star Raiders established, per Barton and Loguidice.
links.added: One-on-one ship duels and a strategy map between alien alliances.

links.took: First-person cockpit space combat that Star Raiders popularized.
links.added: Wingmen, a branching campaign and cutscenes aboard a carrier.
